cover.headline: A good hospital chain at a full price, with the 2018 deal back in court: we initiate with a Sell
cover.lead: Fortis runs 36 facilities with ~6,150 operational beds (incl. ~1,200 managed for others), led by FMRI Gurugram and a dense NCR-Punjab network, and owns 88% of Agilus Diagnostics. Under IHH (31%) it has turned around: operating EBITDA ₹1,101 cr → ₹2,085 cr in FY23-26, margin 17.5% → 22.8%. But growth now depends on new beds (ARPOB +2.6% in Q1FY27, occupancy flat at ~69%), a new ESOP costs ~₹150 cr in FY27, and on 31-Aug-2026 the Delhi High Court ordered a forensic audit of the 2018 IHH deal (the Supreme Court declined to interfere on 25-Sep). The street values Fortis on a **sum of the parts (hospitals 27-30x, diagnostics 23-24x EV/EBITDA)**. We forecast EBITDA of ₹2,301 / 2,743 / 3,178 cr and EPS of ₹14.9 / 19.1 / 23.2 for FY27-29E, below the street on margins. Applying **18.5x to Sep-28E hospital EBITDA and 18x to Agilus** (Fortis's own forward median since 2021, less the sector's de-rating), less ESOP, the Agilus minority and net debt incl. leases, gives **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): we initiate with SELL.** Cross-checks: P/E ₹656, DCF ₹505. Bull case {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear case {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.p: 14 of 24 facilities earn above 20% (70% of revenue) at 74% occupancy; FMRI runs at 85-90%. The turnaround gains are in the numbers; the remaining lever is six ramp-up units with ~10% of revenue and new beds in full hospitals (~1,800 by FY30, only 173 in FY28).

arguments.h: Margins: the target moved, the numbers did not
arguments.p: Hospital margin before ESOP was 21.5% in Q1FY27 (22.1% a year earlier); the 25% FY28 target now has to absorb ~₹120 cr of ESOP. We model 22.6% / 23.4% / 23.8% before ESOP ({{F.ebitdaMargin.0|pct}} / {{F.ebitdaMargin.1|pct}} / {{F.ebitdaMargin.2|pct}} group after it): FY28E EPS 12% below Prabhudas Lilladher.

A forensic audit (report due ~6 months after the 31-Aug-2026 order) re-examines the 2018 IHH investment and the RHT buyback; the Supreme Court questioned hospital drug mark-ups on 29-Sep-2026; CGHS/ECHS drug caps have already cut oncology growth to ~5%. IHH's plans to go to ~50%, inject capital and merge Gleneagles wait on the courts.

arguments.h: Valuation: above peers and its own history
arguments.p: At ₹770 Fortis trades at 22.4x our FY28E EV/EBITDA vs a 21.0x forward median since 2021 and a ~20.3x peer median. The street's ₹1,030-1,150 targets rest on 27-30x hospital multiples: on our estimates those multiples alone give ₹923-1,008.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): first full quarter of the ~₹40 cr ESOP charge; whether the FMRI tower (~200 beds) has opened; hospital margin vs the 25%-by-FY28 path.
The forensic auditor's questionnaire (due ~4 weeks after the 31-Aug-2026 order) and report (~6 months); any appeal or further court steps.
The Supreme Court hearing on hospital drug pricing (adjourned at the 29-Sep-2026 hearing): any move towards a margin cap on medicines.
IHH: terms of any equity infusion, stake increase or Gleneagles merger (needs a majority-of-minority vote).
Agilus under its new CEO (from Jul-2026): test volumes and the 12-13% growth guidance; Manesar oncology (by Nov-2026) and Greater Noida reaching mid-teens margins by end-FY27.

sections.title: A North-India-heavy hospital chain with a national diagnostics arm

blocks.p: Fortis runs multi-specialty hospitals: 36 facilities with 6,150+ operational beds, of which ~4,970 are its own and ~1,200 are managed for others under operations & management (O&M) contracts for a fee. Hospitals earned ₹7,773 cr in FY26 (85% of revenue). The network is concentrated: Delhi NCR (~2,190 beds, led by the flagship Fortis Memorial Research Institute, FMRI, in Gurugram) and Punjab (~990 beds) are half the beds; Bengaluru, Mumbai, Kolkata and Jaipur make up most of the rest. Six specialties (oncology, cardiac, neuro, ortho, gastro and renal) bring 62% of hospital revenue; doctors are mostly paid fees per case, as in most Indian chains.

The second business is **Agilus Diagnostics** (formerly SRL), 88.32% owned: a national pathology chain with 4,493 customer touchpoints, 40.8 mn tests a year and ₹1,527 cr of gross revenue in FY26 (₹171 cr of it from tests for Fortis hospitals). Agilus earned a 23.6% operating margin in FY26 but has grown only ~4% a year since FY23. The controlling shareholder is **IHH Healthcare** of Malaysia (31.17%), Asia's largest listed hospital group, which also owns the Gleneagles hospitals in India that Fortis has managed since Jul-2025.

sections.title: Too few beds, more insurance, and more regulation of what hospitals charge

blocks.p: India has ~16 hospital beds per 10,000 people vs a global average of ~33, and ~14 outside the metros; only ~6% of hospitals are accredited (Crisil, Praxis, via Fortis AR FY26 MD&A). Health-insurance coverage rose from 35% (FY2019) to 41% (FY2024) of the population (Crisil, IRDA); 36% of Fortis's FY26 hospital revenue came through insurers (TPAs) and ~21% from government schemes (CGHS, ECHS, PSUs). These are the reasons Indian hospital chains have grown revenue 13-25% a year and why listed chains are building beds as fast as they can. The other side is price: about a fifth of Fortis's revenue comes from government schemes that set their own rates, insurers negotiate package prices, and in Sep-2026 the Supreme Court openly questioned hospital mark-ups on medicines. Indian diagnostics market ₹860-870 bn in FY24, projected ₹1,275-1,375 bn by FY28 (10-12% a year; Crisil, Axis Capital); still fragmented, with organised chains (Dr Lal, Metropolis, Agilus, Vijaya, Apollo, Redcliffe and online players) gaining share.

sections.title: Revenue = beds × occupancy × ARPOB: beds now do the work, price growth has slowed

blocks.p: Hospital revenue is the product of three numbers: **operational beds**, **occupancy** (share of beds filled) and **ARPOB** (average revenue per occupied bed; Fortis quotes it in ₹ crore per bed per year, on gross revenue). From FY23 to FY26 occupied beds rose 23% (2,665 → 3,270) and ARPOB 25% (₹2.01 cr → ₹2.51 cr), so hospital revenue grew 52%. The mix has flipped: in FY24-25 price did most of the work (ARPOB +11% and +9%); in FY26 and Q1FY27 ARPOB rose only 3.4% and 2.6% while occupied beds jumped 15% and 17%, helped by ~800 beds added in FY26 (acquisitions and brownfield). Occupancy has stayed at 67-72% throughout, which says the new beds are filling. Because ARPOB is on gross revenue, reported revenue is ~5% below occupied beds × ARPOB every year (ratio 0.947 in FY26).

sections.title: Fourteen hospitals earn 70% of revenue at 20%+ margins; six are still ramping up

blocks.p: Fortis does not give profit by hospital, but every quarter it groups facilities by EBITDA margin. In Q1FY27, 14 facilities (3,212 beds) earned more than 20% and brought 70% of hospital revenue, at 74% occupancy and ₹2.71 cr ARPOB; 4 more (809 beds) earned 15-20%, with the highest ARPOB (₹3.19 cr). The tail is 6 facilities (919 beds) below 15%: Yeshwanthpur (People Tree, bought Jan-2026), Manesar (opened Sep-2024) and Greater Noida (leased from Sep-2025) among them, at 54% occupancy and ~₹2 cr ARPOB. Management says the new units cost 0.4pp of margin in Q1FY27 and should add ~1pp once mature; Manesar and Greater Noida are guided to mid-teens margins by end-FY27. A greenfield hospital takes 18-24 months to break even and another year to reach 18-20%; brownfield beds fill almost at once.

sections.title: Agilus: a national lab chain that lost three years; margins are back, growth is not yet

blocks.p: Agilus (SRL until its 2024-25 rebranding) is the second business: pathology and some radiology through 4,493 customer touchpoints and a network of labs, half to consumers (B2C 53% in Q1FY27) and half to hospitals, labs and corporates (B2B). It had a Covid boom (FY22 gross revenue ₹1,605 cr, EBITDA ₹412 cr) and then a long hangover: FY23 revenue −16%, FY24 +2%, FY25 +3%, with the margin at 15-18% after rebranding costs and a contingent payment for an old lab acquisition. FY26 was the first good year (gross revenue +8.5% to ₹1,527 cr, operating margin 23.6%), and Q1FY27 grew 10.2% at 23.9%, but test volumes still rose only 3% (10.46 mn); most of the growth was realisation per test (+7% to ₹387). A new CEO, Vijender Singh, replaced Dr Anand K in Jul-2026 and guides 12-13% growth at 24-25% margins.

blocks.source: GAM research compilation (company filings and calls to Sep-2026)

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict:** Fortis has a real but narrow moat. FMRI and FEHI are destination hospitals with clinical reputations that take decades to build, and the NCR and Punjab clusters give it referral density and cheap brownfield growth. But most of its doctors are fee-for-service and can move (the ESOP is an admission of that), new hospitals in Noida and Gurugram compete for the same patients and doctors, a fifth of revenue comes from government payers who set prices, and Agilus has no edge it has been able to show in growth. Returns on capital (~13% ROCE) are only a little above its cost of capital, which is what a moderate moat looks like.

sections.title: From crisis to 23% margins: revenue 2.3x since FY15, profit only since FY22

blocks.p: Fortis's revenue went from ₹3,966 cr in FY15 to ₹9,128 cr in FY26, but the first half of that decade was lost: under the former promoters the company paid rent on its own hospitals to RHT Health Trust, lent money to promoter entities and lost ₹934 cr in FY18. After IHH took control (Nov-2018) and the hospitals were bought back from RHT (2019), the EBITDA margin rose from 5% (FY19) to 13% (FY20); Covid then swung the numbers (FY21 revenue −13%, FY22 +42% with a testing boom at Agilus). Since FY23 the story has been clean: revenue +13% a year, operating EBITDA ₹1,101 cr → ₹2,085 cr (+24% a year) and margin 17.5% → 22.8%. Profit attributable to shareholders reached ₹1,042 cr in FY26.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the turnaround under IHH is real and mostly done. From here growth has to come from new beds, and the margin is held back by a new ESOP charge, doctor costs in NCR and government drug-price caps.

sections.title: A steady business: Q2 is the strongest quarter, Q1 the richest per bed

blocks.p: Fortis has little seasonality compared with a children's or infectious-disease hospital. The monsoon quarter (Q2, July-September) brings dengue and other medical cases: occupancy peaks (72% in Q2FY25, 71% in Q2FY26) but ARPOB dips because medical patients pay less per day than surgical ones. Q1 (April-June) is surgery-heavy with the highest ARPOB (₹2.71 cr in Q1FY27). Revenue has grown 17-18% year on year in each of the last five quarters, helped by the FY26 acquisitions (Jalandhar from Jul-2025, Greater Noida from Sep-2025, People Tree from Jan-2026).

blocks.p: Over FY25-26 Fortis generated ₹3,025 cr of operating cash. It spent ₹1,792 cr on capex, ₹1,778 cr buying 31% of Agilus from private-equity holders, ₹645 cr on acquisitions and other investments (deal values: Jalandhar ₹462 cr, People Tree ₹430 cr), ₹552 cr on interest and lease payments and ₹187 cr on dividends; the gap was borrowed (₹1,550 cr of NCDs in FY25; net debt excluding leases ₹1,694 cr at Mar-25 and ₹2,334 cr at Mar-26). sections.title: Earnings quality: cleaner than its history, but read the minority, ESOP and exceptional lines

bullets: **Three EBITDA numbers.** Company "operating EBITDA" (₹2,085 cr in FY26) excludes other income and, from Q1FY27, the ESOP charge; "reported EBITDA" in the P&L appendix includes other income, FX and one-offs (₹2,136 cr). Screener's operating profit equals revenue minus expenses, i.e. after ESOP. We model segments before ESOP and deduct the ESOP separately, so model EBITDA matches Screener.

**Leases are small.** Post-Ind AS 116 rent sits in depreciation (₹85 cr right-of-use amortisation) and interest (₹41 cr); lease liabilities are ₹600 cr (₹616 cr at Jun-2026). Pre-Ind AS EBITDA would be ~₹100 cr (1.1pp of revenue) lower. Brokers use reported (post-Ind AS) EBITDA, as we do; leases sit in our net debt.

**Minorities.** 11.68% of Agilus belongs to others: ₹22 cr of FY26 profit (₹235 cr in FY22, before the buyout). We use profit attributable to owners throughout (FORTIS.patch.js) and deduct the Agilus minority in the valuation.

**Exceptional items every year.** FY25 −₹89 cr (associate and asset impairments, partly offset by the Richmond Road gain), FY26 −₹22 cr (Labour Codes ₹55 cr less a ₹33 cr reversal of an associate impairment), Q1FY27 +₹9.5 cr. Screener books them in other income; our forecasts assume none.
**Doctor fees sit outside staff cost.** Professional fees to doctors were ₹1,950 cr (21.4% of revenue) in FY26, on top of ₹1,297 cr (14.2%) of employee cost.
**Cash conversion.** Operating cash flow was 77% of EBITDA in FY26 (90% in FY25); receivable days rose from 33 (FY24) to 42 (FY26) on slower government and insurer payments.

**Goodwill.** ₹4,722 cr (35% of capital employed) from the RHT buyback, SRL/Agilus and FY26 deals; tested every year (key audit matter). Impairments have hit associates (Lanka Hospitals, RHT), not the core.
**Audit.** B S R & Co. (KPMG network); unqualified, with an Emphasis of Matter on the SFIO investigation and other legacy matters from the former promoters' era.

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: AMBER.** The current numbers are well disclosed (segment and hospital-band KPIs every quarter) and cash-backed. Amber because of recurring exceptional items, a new non-cash ESOP charge excluded from the headline "operating EBITDA", a legacy SFIO investigation in the audit report, and rising receivable days.

sections.title: Net debt ₹2,334 cr plus ₹600 cr of leases: comfortable at ~1.1x EBITDA

blocks.p: Fortis owns most of its hospitals since the 2019 RHT buyback, so leases are small for an Indian hospital chain: ₹600 cr of lease liabilities at Mar-2026 (₹280 cr a year earlier; the Greater Noida hospital was taken on a 15-year lease in Sep-2025). Borrowings were ₹2,872 cr (incl. ₹1,550 cr of NCDs raised for the Agilus buyout) against ₹538 cr of cash: net debt ₹2,334 cr excluding leases (1.09x annualised EBITDA), ₹2,580 cr of debt and ₹2,233 cr of net debt at Jun-2026. Goodwill of ₹4,722 cr is 35% of capital employed. Minorities on the balance sheet are only ₹273 cr at book, but the 11.68% of Agilus they own is worth ~₹1,000 cr at our multiple.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a better company than in 2018, but the price already assumes the best case

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** a national hospital network (₹7,773 cr of hospital revenue in FY26), with flagship hospitals in NCR, 68-70% occupancy, a 22% hospital margin, ~1,800 brownfield beds to add by FY30 that its own cash can fund, a controlling shareholder with deep pockets, and an 88% stake in a national lab chain whose margins have recovered.

**What you are paying:** 22.4x our FY28E EV/EBITDA and 40.3x FY28E EPS: above Fortis's own forward medians since 2021 (21.0x and 36.3x) and above the peer median, for ~15% EBITDA growth and a ~12-13% ROE, just as the 2018 deal goes back under a court-ordered forensic audit and the Supreme Court questions hospital drug margins. On the street's method and our inputs the target is {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): **SELL**. P/E (₹656) and DCF (₹505) agree that the price is ahead of the fundamentals.

exhibit.title: Terms used in this report
head: Term
What it means
rows: Beds open and staffed. O&M (operations & management) beds belong to other owners; Fortis runs them for a fee (e.g. 3% of revenue at Gleneagles) and does not consolidate their revenue.
Occupied beds ÷ operational beds, averaged over the period.
Average revenue per occupied bed. Fortis quotes it in ₹ crore per bed per year on gross revenue (₹2.51 cr in FY26 ≈ ₹68,800 per bed-day); reported revenue is ~5% lower.
Average length of stay of an inpatient (days). Fortis does not report it; a broker put it at 4.19 days in Q1FY27.
Adding beds to an existing hospital (new floors or towers) vs building a new hospital on a new site. Brownfield beds fill faster and cost less.
Fortis's quarterly grouping of its hospitals by EBITDA margin band (>20%, 15-20%, 10-15%, <10%).
Company measure: revenue less operating costs, excluding other income and (from Q1FY27) the ESOP charge. Our model EBITDA deducts the ESOP charge.
Employee stock option plan: shares granted to doctors and staff; the fair value is charged to profit over the vesting period (non-cash).
Third-party administrator: processes claims for health insurers; stands for insured patients in the payer mix.
Central Government Health Scheme and Ex-servicemen Contributory Health Scheme: government payers that set package prices and, since FY26, cap chemotherapy drug prices at MRP less 30%.
Tests sold to patients directly vs to hospitals, labs and corporates. B2C is stickier and more profitable.
Agilus collection centres and pick-up points (4,493 at Jun-2026).
Accounting rule that puts leased buildings on the balance sheet: rent becomes depreciation and interest; future rent appears as a lease liability (₹600 cr for Fortis at Mar-2026).
The part of a subsidiary owned by others: 11.68% of Agilus. Their share of profit is not Fortis shareholders' profit.
A court-ordered investigation of transactions; here into the 2016-2018 dissipation of the former promoters' Fortis shares, IHH's 2018 investment and the RHT buyback.
Mandatory tender offer an acquirer must make to minority shareholders under SEBI rules; IHH's, at ₹170 a share, was frozen from 2018 and completed in Nov-2025.
Valuing each business separately (here hospitals and Agilus on EV/EBITDA), then deducting net debt and minorities.
Enterprise value (market value plus net debt, incl. lease liabilities, plus minorities) ÷ EBITDA; share price ÷ earnings per share.
Half of FY28E plus half of FY29E: the 12-month-forward earnings the market will look at in September 2027.
Discounted cash flow valuation; WACC is the required annual return used to discount future cash (here 11.6%, close to the cost of equity because debt is small).
exhibit.source: GAM Research
